0.value:
Averages a set of samples after throwing out the ones that lie too far from the rest - a mean that outliers cannot drag about.

np.mean uses every value, so one glitch pulls it off; np.median ignores glitches but uses only the middle value. np.robust_mean takes the middle road: it finds the values that agree with the majority and averages THOSE. Reach for it to settle on one good estimate from many noisy measurements - a body's shape from many frames of a pose tracker, a resting level from a sensor that occasionally spikes.

HOW IT DECIDES:
It finds the median of the samples, then each sample's distance from the median, and the median of THOSE distances - the MAD (median absolute deviation), a measure of spread that outliers cannot inflate. A sample farther than threshold times the MAD from the median is thrown out; the rest are averaged. With the default threshold 3 a sample must be within 3 MADs. If all the samples are identical the MAD is 0 and they all count. The MAD is used as it is, not scaled up to match a standard deviation: for ordinary noise 1 MAD is about two thirds of a std, so threshold 3 is about 2 std - stricter than it sounds, and a few good samples at the edges are usually dropped too (see the demo).

IT COLLECTS SAMPLES:
Unlike the other averaging nodes, np.robust_mean REMEMBERS. Each 1-D array (or single number) that arrives is added to its store as one more sample, and the result is worked out over everything stored so far. The store keeps the latest 'max samples' (an option, default 1000; 0 keeps everything) - beyond that the oldest are dropped, so a long run follows the recent past. Otherwise it only empties when you click reset, or when a sample of a different length arrives: that starts a new store (with a message in the console), since samples of different lengths cannot be averaged together.
A 2-D array is different: each ROW is taken as one sample and the store is REPLACED by those rows. So a whole batch can be averaged in one go - send it as rows of samples. A plain list of numbers is ONE sample with many parts, not many samples: to average nine single numbers, stand them up as nine rows of one (np.expand_dims 1), as the top demo does.

WHY THE RESULT IS AN ARRAY:
np.mean reduces the array it is given to one number. np.robust_mean does something different: it averages ACROSS the samples it has collected, part by part, so its answer has the shape of ONE SAMPLE - one value for each part. Samples of a single number each give a one-element array, which is why the lists beside the demos show [5.01] rather than 5.01. To use the result as a plain number, take its first element with np.[] 0.

SAMPLES WITH SEVERAL PARTS:
Each part (column) is averaged separately, but a sample is thrown out WHOLE if ANY of its parts is an outlier - a frame with one bad joint is dropped entirely, which keeps its other parts from leaking in.

SYNTAX:
np.robust_mean <threshold: float>
Default threshold 3.0.

EXAMPLE:
np.robust_mean 3

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

in:
A sample (1-D array, list or number) to add, or a 2-D array of samples to replace the store with. Every arrival sends a new result. A bang sends the result again from the stored samples without adding one - use it after changing threshold.

threshold (drag float, also an inlet):
How many MADs from the median a sample may be and still count. Lower is stricter. Changing it does NOT send by itself: the demo's float goes through 't bang float', which sets threshold and then bangs in.

reset (button):
Empties the store.

samples (shown on the node):
How many samples are stored. It is a display - a typed value snaps back to the count.

max samples (option, default 1000):
The most samples kept; beyond it the oldest are dropped. 0 keeps every sample until reset.

OUTPUTS:

robust mean:
An array as long as one sample - the average of the samples kept. With a single sample stored it is that sample. If the threshold is so strict that no sample survives, the median is sent instead.

inlier count:
How many samples were kept. Worth watching: if it falls far below the number stored, the threshold is too strict (or the data is mostly bad).

THE OUTLIER (top demo):
Nine readings, eight close to 5 and a glitch of 20, sent as nine samples of one value each. np.mean says 6.68, np.median 5.1; np.robust_mean drops the 20 and averages the other eight: 5.01, inlier count 8. Drag the glitch anywhere above about 5.7 and the result does not move. Drag it down to 5 - no glitch at all - and the count drops to 7, not 9: the readings are now so close that 4.7 and 5.3 count as outliers. Lower threshold to 1.5 and the readings farthest from 5.1 are dropped too (count 6); raise it to 100 and nothing is dropped - the result becomes the plain mean.

COLLECTING (lower demo):
The slider sends one number per move, and each is stored as a sample;
watch samples count up. Hold it around one place for a while, then flick it far away and straight back: the few samples the flick added are outliers, and the robust mean stays where you held it. Click reset on the node to start again.

RELATED:
np.mean averages everything; np.median takes the middle value. np.std measures spread with the mean and the squared distances, which an outlier inflates - the MAD used here is its sturdy counterpart. np.nanmean skips missing values, but keeps wrong ones.
